reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey gives the clearest measured figure for this sector. Under "Other services," the NAICS 81 grouping that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, 15.0% of firms answered Yes to whether they had used AI in the last two weeks, up from 13.7% in the prior period. The series first asked the question in September 2023. That is the only hard adoption number in the material, and it covers a broader services category rather than nonprofits alone.

On what AI is actually used for, the Center for Effective Philanthropy is the source that speaks to deployment. Its sector research, including AI-focused reporting, examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. CEP also runs assessments that gather feedback from grantees, donors, and funder staff and benchmark results against other grantmakers, and it publishes an annual State of Nonprofits report. Beyond that description, the excerpts do not quantify which functions dominate or how spending breaks down.

The funding and infrastructure picture is thin. Candid, the nonprofit data organization behind GuideStar and Foundation Center, tracks grantmaking trends including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure, and its page notes that operating on a high moral and ethical plane while keeping a brand strong has become more complicated in the age of AI. The World of AI's own ecosystem catalogue lists four individually verified nonprofits and open source foundations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations, and states plainly that none are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense. It names LMSYS, which stewards Chatbot Arena as shared evaluation infrastructure, Khan Academy as an end-user of AI in education, and the Krita and Blender foundations as stewards of creative tools that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. The same page states the list carries no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights, and that the notes confirm organizational structure and nonprofit status but not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

On access and skills, the AI Equity Project describes building structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs to make AI accessible, ethical, and practical, transforming public libraries and community spaces into learning environments that pair senior citizens with student volunteers, and operating a global network that provides standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities. NTEN frames the same territory as an equity problem, stating that nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector that must be dismantled, and it runs sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption, plus certificates, scholarships, and an Equity Guide practitioners can pledge to use. Stanford HAI's AI Index is cited as the citable macro series on AI's social impact and implementation across mission-driven and public-sector organizations.

The sources do not report ROI figures for nonprofit AI deployment. No excerpt in this material gives a return, a cost saving, or a measured outcome from an AI implementation, and no vendor or pricing concentration is quantified. What the material does show about constraints is qualitative: CEP's research is framed around a sector in crisis and foundations evolving their responses, and its commentary notes that funding is getting harder to come by and the political landscape is not making mission-driven work easier. NTEN's emphasis on equity and the AI Equity Project's emphasis on access point to capability gaps rather than returns.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the honest summary from this material is that adoption is real but modest, with the Census Bureau putting the broader services category at 15.0%, and that the documented activity clusters around operations, program delivery, and communications rather than infrastructure. The supporting ecosystem is small, four catalogued organizations, and the sources are explicit that governance detail, funding scale, and compute access are not captured there. The recurring themes across CEP, NTEN, the AI Equity Project, and Candid are capacity and equity, not proven financial return, so a deployment decision here rests on mission fit and staff capability more than on an ROI case these sources provide.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid describes itself as a provider of grants and nonprofit data intended to help people find funding, research nonprofits and connect with funders. It says analysts, advocates and philanthropists use its information to build a broad picture of social sector activity, and it invites readers to learn how it collects, organises and distributes that data. The page also flags several topics it covers: the conditions attached to most grant funding and some donations, and the strain those conditions place on nonprofits; one foundation's stated reasons for sharing its grantmaking data with Candid, which it frames as a matter of transparency; and the argument that recognition, media coverage, partnerships and growth do not by themselves make a nonprofit financially sustainable, since it needs ongoing unrestricted support. It notes that impact evaluations are growing in importance for nonprofits and funders alike, and offers an email list for insights, trends, product updates and research.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues four individually verified organisations classified as nonprofits or open-source foundations, each checked against a document the organisation published about itself, with the source and its last-read date recorded. It states that two are nonprofits and two are open-source foundations whose roles touch AI tooling and evaluation, though none build compute or power infrastructure. LMSYS is described as the most AI-central entry, stewarding a shared evaluation platform used by the wider AI community to benchmark model quality, while Khan Academy is characterised as an end-user of AI in education rather than a producer, and the Krita and Blender foundations as stewards of creative software whose missions predate AI. The page notes what it does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-centre specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights publicly, with the notes confirming only organisational structure and nonprofit status rather than funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
